extracted.intended_audience: employers and industry stakeholders affected by OSHA's proposed heat standard; policymakers, regulators, and economic analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the proposed OSHA heat standard's substantive compliance requirements (training, monitoring, HIIPP, recordkeeping, employee involvement) and the operational assumptions OSHA used to estimate costs. Focused on employer duties under the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping — indoor work area measurements retention
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard would require that indoor work area measurements be retained for 6 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes employers would purchase a wireless temperature and humidity data logger (described in section VIII.C.IV.C.) to meet this requirement. Since data loggers can automatically record heat index measurements, OSHA assumes employers would incur no additional cost to comply with this recordkeeping requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring environmental conditions (indoor and outdoor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishments would be expected to monitor environmental conditions in and around work areas under the proposed standard for both indoor and outdoor work sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For outdoor work sites, establishments could track local forecasts to meet this requirement; for indoor sites, OSHA assumes use of temperature and data loggers. OSHA assumes one work area per establishment for the analysis and estimates indoor vs. outdoor establishments by industry based on employee location percentages. Unit costs differ for indoor vs. outdoor monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of heat-exposed indoor work areas and periodic reevaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Indoor establishments would also need to identify work areas that pose heat-related risks to employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes 20 percent of establishments will need to reevaluate work areas due to process changes every year, leading to an assumed reevaluation at each establishment every five years (costs incurred in year 1 and year 6 for present-value calculation). Employee involvement in work-area evaluations is required (see separate employee involvement metric). OSHA annualized these periodic costs (2% discount rate over 10 years) for inclusion in total annualized costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Plan (HIIPP) development requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All affected establishments would incur costs for developing a HIIPP. Establishments that already have a HIIPP are expected to review and make any modifications necessary to match the requirements outlined in this proposed standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed standard does not require establishments with ten or less employees to develop their HIIPP in writing. OSHA assumed establishments without an existing HIIPP and with more than ten employees would choose one of three options: (1) write a HIIPP from scratch (10% assumed), (2) use OSHA's template (90% assumed as the less burdensome option), or (3) have no written HIIPP if applicable to small establishments. Affected establishments must review and update their HIIPPs annually (time estimate: one hour). Tables (VIII.C.22) show industry-level one-time and annualized costs for each option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee involvement in HIIPP development, review, and update
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard would require that non-managerial employees be involved in the development, review, and update of the HIIPP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumed four employees per establishment would spend one hour providing input on HIIPP development and 20 minutes on the review and update of their establishment's HIIPP. These time estimates are assumed to be the same regardless of whether the establishment uses the OSHA template or writes a HIIPP from scratch. Tables present annualized costs associated with employee involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee involvement in work-area evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee participation is required for identification and reevaluation of heat-exposed work areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumed four employees per establishment would participate as a representative sample to provide input during work-area evaluations. Because evaluations are assumed to occur every five years, OSHA calculated present value assuming costs in year 1 and year 6 then annualized (2% discount over 10 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirements — initial and recurring trainings
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard requires initial and recurring trainings for different roles (designated person, at-risk worker, supervisors, and persons developing supervisor training).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM provides detailed tables of assumed hours and costs by industry and role. Headings and table entries include: 'Initial Employee Training—Designated Person' (one-time; table shows e.g., 4.0 hours in many entries), 'Initial Employee Training—At-Risk Worker' (one-time; e.g., 1.0 hour), 'Initial Supervisor Training Development' (one-time; e.g., 2.0 hours), 'Initial Supervisor Training—Supervisor' (one-time; e.g., 1.25 hours), and 'Initial Supervisor Training—Designated Person' (one-time; e.g., 1.0 hour). Recurring trainings include 'Annual Employee Refresher Training—Designated Person' (annual; e.g., 0.75 hours), 'Annual Employee Refresher Training—At-Risk Worker' (annual; e.g., 0.50 hours), 'Annual Supervisor Refresher Training—Supervisor' (annual; e.g., 0.63 hours), and 'Annual Supervisor Refresher Training—Designated Person' (annual; e.g., 0.5 hours). The tables also show 'Supplemental Employee Refresher Training' and 'Supplemental Supervisor Refresher Training' with similar hour assumptions. Industry-specific unit costs and total annualized costs are presented in the NPRM tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring equipment purchase and user manual review
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers are assumed to purchase monitoring equipment (wireless temperature and humidity data loggers) and review associated user manuals to implement indoor monitoring requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's analysis includes line items for 'Monitoring Equipment—Indoor' (one-time annualized costs) and 'Review Monitoring Equipment User Manual—Indoor' with industry-specific cost estimates. OSHA assumes data loggers can automatically record heat index measurements, and includes the unit costs in the cost tables (see Table VIII.C.23 and related subtables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule familiarization obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: All affected establishments would incur rule familiarization costs to learn and understand the proposed standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA multiplies the number of affected establishments by unit costs shown in table VIII.C.8 to calculate total rule familiarization cost. As all affected employers incur this cost, no compliance adjustment is applied. Table VIII.C.21 shows annualized one-time, annual, and total annualized costs by industry (discounted at 2% over 10 years and undiscounted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to use OSHA HIIPP template vs. write plan from scratch
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishments without an existing HIIPP may choose between using OSHA's template or writing a HIIPP from scratch; small establishments (≤10 employees) may use an unwritten HIIPP guided by the template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the cost analysis OSHA assumed 90% of establishments without an existing plan (and >10 employees) would use the OSHA template and 10% would write from scratch. The NPRM provides separate cost subtotals for 'Write HIIPP from Scratch', 'Review and Modify HIIPP—Existing Plan in Place', 'Use HIIPP Template', and 'No Written HIIPP' (for small establishments). Each option has industry-specific one-time and annualized costs shown in Table VIII.C.22.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions for cost annualization and timing of periodic costs
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA annualized one-time costs using a 2 percent discount rate over a 10-year period. Two costs that occur every five years were treated as incurred in year 1 and year 6, discounted at 2 percent, and then annualized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annualized one-time and annual costs, plus the annualized periodic costs, are summed to estimate total annualized costs. For each provision, OSHA also calculated undiscounted annualized costs assuming a 0 percent discount rate over 10 years. These methodological choices drive the presented annualized cost figures in the tables.
